# SK2200 — The field initializer is overwritten by every constructor

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

A private instance field is given a value at its declaration and every constructor that runs field initializers assigns it again before anything reads it, so the declared value never survives an allocation.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Correctness |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, safe |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |
| ReSharper | `MemberInitializerValueIgnored` (`resharper_member_initializer_value_ignored_highlighting`) |

## Why

The initializer is dead work on every allocation, and that is the smaller half. The larger half is that two values are written down for one field and only one of them is ever true, so a reader who looks at the declaration to learn the default learns a value the program never holds. ⚠ **Which of the two was meant is a real question and the finding does not answer it.** What it asserts is narrower and checkable: the value at the declaration is unreachable. Deleting it is the edit that makes the code say what it does; keeping it and deleting the constructor's assignment is the other repair, and only the author knows which.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
sealed class Session {
    readonly int retries = 5;   // never survives a single allocation

    public Session(int given) => retries = given;
}
```

Write:

```csharp
sealed class Session {
    readonly int retries;

    public Session(int given) => retries = given;
}
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **Only a constructor that actually runs field initializers counts.** C# runs them in constructors that do not chain to `this(…)`, so a chaining constructor is evidence of nothing and is skipped; the rule fires only when *every* non-chaining constructor overwrites the field. A type with no explicitly declared instance constructor is never examined, because the implicit one writes nothing at all. ⚠ **A record, a primary constructor and any constructor Roslyn declared implicitly stop the walk for the whole type**, because a record's copy constructor does not run field initializers and a primary constructor's assignments are not constructor statements the walk can read — in both the shape of the evidence is different from the shape the rule checks. ⚠ **The write has to be the first thing that touches the field.** It must be a plain `x = …` or `this.x = …` at the top level of the constructor body, and every statement before it must neither mention the field nor contain an invocation, an object creation, `this` or `base`, any of which could read the initialized value before it is overwritten and so make it observable. A constructor initializer whose arguments mention the field declines for the same reason. ⚠ **A field referenced from an `override` member is declined, and this is the guard easiest to leave out.** Field initializers run *before* the base constructor call, so a base constructor that calls a virtual method this type overrides can read the initialized value — and there the initializer is not dead at all. ⚠ **The initializer itself must be side-effect free, because the fix deletes it**: literals, `default`, `nameof`, `typeof`, `sizeof`, a chain of names, a cast, a unary operator and parentheses over those. `= new List<int>()` is declined — an allocation whose constructor registers something is exactly what `SK2013` and `CA1806` argue about, and this rule will not delete a `new` on its own authority. Private instance fields only; `const`, `static` and non-private fields are out of scope, and an auto-property initializer with the same defect is an under-report this rule documents rather than covers. A span carrying a comment or a preprocessor directive is not reported at all, rather than reported without the fix the catalogue promises. Generated code is excluded.
